claim: Malaria is a serious infectious disease caused by mosquito-transmitted protozoan parasites of the genus Plasmodium.
source: Malaria is a serious infectious disease caused by mosquito-transmitted protozoan parasites of the genus Plasmodium.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about malaria etiology.

claim: At least five species of Plasmodium parasites can cause disease in humans.
source: At least five species of these parasites can cause disease in humans, but by far the most serious is Plasmodium falciparum.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Plasmodium species.

claim: Plasmodium falciparum is the most serious species of malaria parasite.
source: At least five species of these parasites can cause disease in humans, but by far the most serious is Plasmodium falciparum.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about P. falciparum.

claim: Plasmodium falciparum was responsible for an estimated 241 million disease episodes in 2020.
source: This parasite alone was responsible for an estimated 241 million disease episodes and 627,000 deaths in 2020, mainly in sub-Saharan Africa (WHO, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO 2021 report.

claim: Plasmodium falciparum was responsible for an estimated 627,000 deaths in 2020.
source: This parasite alone was responsible for an estimated 241 million disease episodes and 627,000 deaths in 2020, mainly in sub-Saharan Africa (WHO, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO 2021 report.

claim: Malaria deaths in 2020 occurred mainly in sub-Saharan Africa.
source: This parasite alone was responsible for an estimated 241 million disease episodes and 627,000 deaths in 2020, mainly in sub-Saharan Africa (WHO, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO 2021 report.

claim: Acquired immunity to P. falciparum malaria following natural exposure is mediated mainly by IgG antibodies with specificity for the asexual blood stages of the infection.
source: Acquired immunity to P. falciparum malaria following natural exposure is mediated mainly by IgG antibodies with specificity for the asexual blood stages of the infection (Cohen et al., 1961; Sabchareon et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cohen et al., 1961 and Sabchareon et al., 1991.

claim: Acquisition of protection to P. falciparum malaria following natural exposure takes years to develop.
source: However, acquisition of protection following natural exposure takes years to develop, and complete protection is rarely if ever achieved (reviewed by Hviid, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to review by Hviid, 2005.

claim: Complete protection to P. falciparum malaria is rarely if ever achieved following natural exposure.
source: However, acquisition of protection following natural exposure takes years to develop, and complete protection is rarely if ever achieved (reviewed by Hviid, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to review by Hviid, 2005.

claim: The extensive inter-clonal polymorphism and intra-clonal variation of key parasite antigens appear to be important reasons for slow acquisition of immunity.
source: The extensive inter-clonal polymorphism and intra-clonal variation of key parasite antigens appear to be important reasons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the context of slow immunity acquisition.

claim: The identification of conserved and functionally important antibody epitopes in key antigens is a major goal of malaria immunology research.
source: Consequently, the identification of conserved and functionally important antibody epitopes in key antigens is a major goal of malaria immunology research.
evidence: This is a statement about research goals in the field.

claim: Conventional approaches such as ELISA have difficulty separating true from apparent cross-reactivity.
source: However, it is a goal that is difficult to achieve using conventional approaches such as analysis of immune sera by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). A major obstacle is the inability to separating true (i.e., a single antibody that recognizes a conserved epitope shared by multiple allelic variants; Figure 1A) from apparent cross-reactivity (multiple antibodies, each recognizing a variant-specific epitope; Figure 1B), because this requires analysis at the single B-cell level.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of ELISA methodology.

claim: Separating true from apparent cross-reactivity requires analysis at the single B-cell level.
source: A major obstacle is the inability to separating true (i.e., a single antibody that recognizes a conserved epitope shared by multiple allelic variants; Figure 1A) from apparent cross-reactivity (multiple antibodies, each recognizing a variant-specific epitope; Figure 1B), because this requires analysis at the single B-cell level.
evidence: This is a logical inference about methodological requirements.

claim: The B-cell ELISpot assay was developed by Czerkinsky et al. in 1983.
source: The development of a B-cell ELISpot assay was a first step toward that (Czerkinsky et al., 1983).
evidence: Supported by citation to Czerkinsky et al., 1983.

claim: In the ELISpot assay, each spot corresponds to the antibodies secreted by a single B-cell.
source: In the assay, each spot corresponds to the antibodies secreted by a single B-cell, that is, to a monoclonal antibody.
evidence: This is established knowledge about how ELISpot assays work.

claim: The ELISpot assay has been modified to allow detection of antibody-secreting B cells by fluorescence and concomitant detection of several antibody specificities (reverse FluoroSpot).
source: The ELISpot assay has since been modified to allow detection of the antibody-secreting B cells (ASCs) by fluorescence and concomitant detection of several antibody specificities (reverse FluoroSpot) (Hadjilaou et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hadjilaou et al., 2015.

claim: Further modifications of the FluoroSpot assay enabled the determination of antibody cross-reactivity against different dengue serotypes and closely related viruses.
source: Further modifications enabled the determination of antibody cross-reactivity against different dengue serotypes and closely related viruses (Adam et al., 2018), and a versatile adaptation of the assay to antigens of choice (Jahnmatz et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Adam et al., 2018.

claim: A versatile adaptation of the FluoroSpot assay to antigens of choice was developed by Jahnmatz et al. in 2016.
source: Further modifications enabled the determination of antibody cross-reactivity against different dengue serotypes and closely related viruses (Adam et al., 2018), and a versatile adaptation of the assay to antigens of choice (Jahnmatz et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jahnmatz et al., 2016.

claim: VAR2CSA-type PfEMP1 is a notoriously polymorphic antigen involved in the pathogenesis of placental malaria.
source: Using VAR2CSA-type PfEMP1—a notoriously polymorphic antigen involved in the pathogenesis of placental malaria—as a model, we demonstrate the robustness of the assay and its applicability to analysis of true cross-reactivity of monoclonal VAR2CSA-specific antibodies in naturally exposed individuals.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VAR2CSA.

claim: The developed FluoroSpot assay demonstrates robustness for analysis of true cross-reactivity of monoclonal VAR2CSA-specific antibodies in naturally exposed individuals.
source: Using VAR2CSA-type PfEMP1—a notoriously polymorphic antigen involved in the pathogenesis of placental malaria—as a model, we demonstrate the robustness of the assay and its applicability to analysis of true cross-reactivity of monoclonal VAR2CSA-specific antibodies in naturally exposed individuals.
evidence: This is a claim about the study's findings, supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The assay is adaptable to the analysis of other polymorphic antigens.
source: The assay is adaptable to the analysis of other polymorphic antigens, rendering it a powerful tool in studies of immunity to malaria and many other diseases.
evidence: This is an inference based on the design and validation of the assay.

claim: VAR2CSA is responsible for the accumulation of infected erythrocytes in the placenta.
source: VAR2CSA is responsible for the accumulation of infected erythrocytes (IEs) in the placenta (Salanti et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Salanti et al., 2004.

claim: Placental malaria affects about a third of all pregnancies in malaria-endemic areas.
source: This can lead to placental malaria, which affects about a third of all pregnancies in malaria-endemic areas and is the direct cause of substantial maternal, fetal, and infant morbidity (WHO, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO, 2021.

claim: Placental malaria is the direct cause of substantial maternal, fetal, and infant morbidity.
source: This can lead to placental malaria, which affects about a third of all pregnancies in malaria-endemic areas and is the direct cause of substantial maternal, fetal, and infant morbidity (WHO, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO, 2021.

claim: Vaccines based on the minimal binding domain of VAR2CSA induced a variant-specific rather than cross-reactive antibody response.
source: It was recently reported that vaccines, based on the minimal binding domain that is assumed to be a functionally conserved region of VAR2CSA mediating placental IE sequestration by binding to oncofetal chondroitin sulfate A (CSA), induced a variant-specific rather than cross-reactive antibody response (Mordmüller et al., 2019; Sirima et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mordmüller et al., 2019 and Sirima et al., 2020.

claim: Recombinant proteins corresponding to four allelic variants (IT4, NF54, M920, and Malayan Camp) of the ID1-ID2, DBL3X, and DBL5ε regions of P. falciparum VAR2CSA were produced in human embryonic kidney cells.
source: We produced recombinant proteins corresponding to four allelic variants (IT4, NF54, M920, and Malayan Camp) of the ID1-ID2, DBL3X, and DBL5ε regions of P. falciparum VAR2CSA in human embryonic kidney cells.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Each recombinant antigen included one of four peptide tags (GAL, TRAP, TWIN, and WASP) to enable 'plug-and-play' detection.
source: Each recombinant antigen included one of four peptide tags (GAL, TRAP, TWIN, and WASP) to enable 'plug-and-play' detection with standard, tag-specific, and fluorescently labeled reagents (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the experimental design, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: All the recombinant proteins appeared as single bands at the expected sizes in Instant Blue-stained SDS-PAGE gels.
source: All the recombinant proteins appeared as single bands at the expected sizes in Instant Blue-stained SDS-PAGE gels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: All the recombinant antigens were specifically recognized in the sex-specific manner typical of VAR2CSA when tested in ELISA.
source: All the recombinant antigens were specifically recognized in the sex-specific manner (recognized by plasma IgG from P. falciparum-exposed women but not from sympatric men) typical of VAR2CSA (Fried et al., 1998; Ricke et al., 2000; Salanti et al., 2004), when tested in ELISA (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and citations.

claim: Each of the differently tagged versions of IT4 ID1-ID2 reacted identically with the different plasma IgG pools.
source: Each of the differently tagged versions of IT4 ID1-ID2 reacted identically with the different plasma IgG pools (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The mouse monoclonal antibody 6E2 reacted with the IT4, NF54, and M920 allelic variants of ID1-ID2, but did not react with Malayan Camp ID1-ID2.
source: The mouse monoclonal antibody 6E2, derived from a mouse immunized with recombinant IT4 ID1-ID2 (unpublished data), reacted with the IT4, NF54, and M920 allelic variants of ID1-ID2, but did not react with Malayan Camp ID1-ID2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The DBL3X-specific human monoclonal antibodies PAM2.8 and PAM8.1 reacted with all four allelic variants of DBL3X.
source: The DBL3X-specific human monoclonal antibodies PAM2.8 and PAM8.1 reacted with all four allelic variants of DBL3X, although PAM8.1 recognized NF54 DBL3X is less well than the other variants.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from ELISA experiments.

claim: PAM8.1 recognized NF54 DBL3X less well than the other variants.
source: The DBL3X-specific human monoclonal antibodies PAM2.8 and PAM8.1 reacted with all four allelic variants of DBL3X, although PAM8.1 recognized NF54 DBL3X is less well than the other variants.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from ELISA experiments.

claim: The DBL5ε-specific human monoclonal antibody PAM3.10 recognized all four variants of VAR2CSA-DBL5ε equally well.
source: The DBL5ε-specific human monoclonal antibody PAM3.10 recognized all four variants of VAR2CSA-DBL5ε equally well.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from ELISA experiments.

claim: PAM1.4 did not recognize any of the VAR2CSA region constructs.
source: PAM1.4, reported to recognize a conserved, but conformational and probably discontinuous epitope in VAR2SCA (Barfod et al., 2007), did not recognize any of the VAR2CSA region constructs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and citation.

claim: All the tested antibodies, including PAM1.4, recognized a recombinant protein representing the full ectodomain of IT4 VAR2CSA.
source: All the tested antibodies, including PAM1.4, recognized a recombinant protein representing the full ectodomain of IT4 VAR2CSA (also known as IT4VAR04).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from ELISA experiments.

claim: A DBL4ε domain from a non-VAR2CSA PfEMP1 protein was not recognized by any of the monoclonal antibodies.
source: A DBL4ε domain from a non-VAR2CSA PfEMP1 protein was not recognized by any of the monoclonal antibodies, underscoring their VAR2CSA-specificity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from ELISA experiments.

claim: Most of the tagged proteins were recognized exclusively by the detection reagent corresponding to the incorporated tag.
source: Most of the tagged proteins were recognized exclusively by the detection reagent corresponding to the incorporated tag.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from ELISA experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The TRAP-specific detection reagent showed minor cross-reactivity with the WASP-tagged Malayan Camp DBL3X antigen.
source: However, the TRAP-specific detection reagent showed minor cross-reactivity with the WASP-tagged Malayan Camp DBL3X antigen and the M920 DBL5ε allelic variant was not well recognized.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from ELISA experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The M920 DBL5ε allelic variant was not well recognized by the tag detection reagents.
source: However, the TRAP-specific detection reagent showed minor cross-reactivity with the WASP-tagged Malayan Camp DBL3X antigen and the M920 DBL5ε allelic variant was not well recognized.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from ELISA experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: For each matching tag/detection reagent combination, similar numbers of spots were detected in the 1×1 configuration.
source: For each matching tag/detection reagent combination (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), we detected similar numbers of spots, each corresponding to a 6E2-secreting hybridoma cell (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Spots were exclusively detected in the instrument channel corresponding to the detection reagent used in the 1×1 configuration.
source: Spots were exclusively detected in the instrument channel corresponding to the detection reagent used (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Only single-colored spots of the expected color were detected in the 1×1 configuration.
source: In other words, only single-colored spots of the expected color were detected.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the FluoroSpot assay.

claim: Detection in the 1×1 configuration was highly specific and independent of the tag/detection reagent combination used.
source: Detection was highly specific and independent of the tag/detection reagent combination used.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in the 1×1 configuration.

claim: In each of the 1×4 configurations, spots were exclusively detected in the correct channel.
source: In each of the 1×4 configurations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), spots were exclusively detected in the correct channel (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), with similar spot counts among the different 1×4 designs and corresponding to the results obtained with the 1×1 design (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A and 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The presence of multiple detection reagents did not affect assay performance in the 1×4 configuration.
source: The results document that the presence of multiple detection reagents did not affect assay performance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing 1×1 and 1×4 configurations.

claim: In each of the four complementary 4×1 configurations, spots were exclusively detected in the correct channel.
source: In each of the four complementary (4×1) configurations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), again spots were exclusively detected in the correct channel (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), with similar spot counts regardless of the detection reagent used, and corresponding to the results obtained with the 1×1 and 1×4 configurations (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A and 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The simultaneous use of multiple tagged versions of the same antigen did not affect assay performance in the 4×1 configuration.
source: The results document that the simultaneous use of multiple tagged versions of the same antigen did not affect assay performance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing different configurations.

claim: In the 4×4 configuration, similar numbers of spots were detected as in the 1×1, 1×4, and 4×1 configurations.
source: As in the previous configurations, we detected similar numbers of spots (Figure 2B), corresponding closely to those detected in the 1×1, 1×4, and 4×1 configurations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Most of the spots in the 4×4 configuration were detected by at least two (and primarily by four) of the tag detection reagents.
source: Of note, most of the spots were detected by at least two (and primarily by four) of the tag detection reagents (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: RSV values were consistently higher for configurations with only one tagged antigen (1×1 and 1×4) than configurations with differently tagged versions of the antigen (4×1 and 4×4).
source: Although spot numbers were consistent in all configurations, RSV values were consistently higher for configurations with only one tagged antigen (1×1 and 1×4) than configurations with differently tagged versions of the antigen (4×1 and 4×4) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The difference in RSV values between configurations likely reflects competition among the differently tagged versions of the IT4 ID1-ID2 antigen for binding to captured 6E2 antibodies.
source: This likely reflects competition among the differently tagged versions of the IT4 ID1-ID2 antigen for binding to captured 6E2 antibodies when all versions were added together.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: An apparent higher level of background signal was consistently observed in the LED380 detection channel.
source: We consistently observed an apparent higher level of background signal in the LED380 detection channel, evidenced by a ring of blue fluorescence at the edge and the center of the wells that occasionally generated an increase in the number of single-positive spots in this channel (likely false positives).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The FluoroSpot assay produced reliable and consistent results, regardless of the complexity of multiplexing.
source: We conclude from these experiments that our FluoroSpot assay produced reliable and consistent results, regardless of the complexity of multiplexing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the validation experiments.

claim: When all four allelic variants of ID1-ID2 were tested with 6E2 antibody in the 4×4 configuration, spots were only detected with the IT4 allele reagent (TWIN) and M920 allele reagent (WASP).
source: When all four allelic variants of ID1-ID2 and all four detection reagents were added to secreted and captured 6E2 antibody (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), spots were only detected with the IT4 allele reagent (TWIN) and M920 allele reagent (WASP) (Figure 3A), indicating the presence of a strongly 6E2-crossreactive epitope present in IT4 and M920, which is absent from NF54 and Malayan Camp.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There is a strongly 6E2-crossreactive epitope present in IT4 and M920 ID1-ID2, which is absent from NF54 and Malayan Camp.
source: When all four allelic variants of ID1-ID2 and all four detection reagents were added to secreted and captured 6E2 antibody (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), spots were only detected with the IT4 allele reagent (TWIN) and M920 allele reagent (WASP) (Figure 3A), indicating the presence of a strongly 6E2-crossreactive epitope present in IT4 and M920, which is absent from NF54 and Malayan Camp.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Most of the detected spots with 6E2 and ID1-ID2 variants were double-positive.
source: This conclusion was supported by the fact that most of the detected spots were double-positive.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the FluoroSpot assay.

claim: RSV values for 6E2 with different allelic variants of ID1-ID2 were less affected by multiplexing than when assaying 6E2 with differently tagged versions of the same ID1-ID2 allele (IT4).
source: In agreement with the only partial cross-reactivity of 6E2 with the different allelic variants of ID1-ID2, RSV values were less affected by multiplexing (Figure 3C) than when assaying 6E2 with differently tagged versions of the same ID1-ID2 allele (IT4) (Figure 2C), consistent with a lower degree of antigen competition for bound antibody.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2C and 3C.

claim: Detection of true allelic cross-reactivity of monoclonal antibodies is possible with the FluoroSpot assay.
source: These results show that detection of true allelic cross-reactivity of monoclonal antibodies is possible with the FluoroSpot assay, although some low-affinity cross-reactivity might be missed.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the validation experiments with 6E2 and ID1-ID2 variants.

claim: Some low-affinity cross-reactivity might be missed with the FluoroSpot assay.
source: These results show that detection of true allelic cross-reactivity of monoclonal antibodies is possible with the FluoroSpot assay, although some low-affinity cross-reactivity might be missed.
evidence: This is a caveat noted based on the experimental observations.

claim: The PAM2.8-secreting clone produced spots that could be detected with all four allelic variants of DBL3X in the 4×4 configuration.
source: In the fully multiplexed 4×4 configuration of the assay (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), the PAM2.8-secreting clone produced spots that could be detected with all four allelic variants of DBL3X, with most spots reacting with three or four of the detection reagents (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Most PAM2.8 spots reacted with three or four of the detection reagents.
source: In the fully multiplexed 4×4 configuration of the assay (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), the PAM2.8-secreting clone produced spots that could be detected with all four allelic variants of DBL3X, with most spots reacting with three or four of the detection reagents (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The PAM8.1 antibody reacted with the IT4, M920, and Malayan Camp allelic variants of DBL3X, but was non-reactive with NF54 DBL3X.
source: The PAM8.1 antibody reacted with the IT4, M920, and Malayan Camp allelic variants of DBL3X, but was non-reactive with NF54 DBL3X as expected, since this particular variant lacks the linear epitope recognized by PAM8.1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the FluoroSpot assay.

claim: NF54 DBL3X lacks the linear epitope recognized by PAM8.1.
source: The PAM8.1 antibody reacted with the IT4, M920, and Malayan Camp allelic variants of DBL3X, but was non-reactive with NF54 DBL3X as expected, since this particular variant lacks the linear epitope recognized by PAM8.1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the PAM8.1 epitope.

claim: Most PAM8.1 spots reacted with two or three detection reagents.
source: Most spots reacted with two or three detection reagents (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: PAM3.10 cross-reacted with all four allelic variants of DBL5ε.
source: In the same assay configuration, but employing allelic variants of DBL5ε rather than DBL3X (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), PAM3.10 was shown to cross-react with all four allelic variants DBL5ε, and mainly produced spots reacting with three or four of the detection reagents (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: PAM3.10 mainly produced spots reacting with three or four of the detection reagents.
source: In the same assay configuration, but employing allelic variants of DBL5ε rather than DBL3X (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), PAM3.10 was shown to cross-react with all four allelic variants DBL5ε, and mainly produced spots reacting with three or four of the detection reagents (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: No spots were observed when testing the PAM1.4-secreting clone in the FluoroSpot assay (4×4 configuration) with any of the DBL3X or DBL5ε allelic variants.
source: We did not observe any spots when testing the PAM1.4-secreting clone in the FluoroSpot assay (4×4 configuration) with any of our DBL3X or DBL5ε allelic variants (data not shown).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The FluoroSpot assay results with human monoclonal antibodies were consistent with those obtained with ELISA.
source: All these results were consistent with those obtained with ELISA (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) and with previous reports on the specificity of these monoclonal antibodies (Barfod et al., 2007; Barfod et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a comparison of results from different experimental methods and citations.

claim: RSV values were consistently higher for configurations with only a single tagged allelic variant (1×1 and 1×4) than for configurations with multiple, differently tagged allelic variants of the antigen present (4×1 and 4×4) for human monoclonal antibodies.
source: RSV values were consistently higher for configurations with only a single tagged allelic variant (1×1 and 1×4) than for configurations with multiple, differently tagged allelic variants of the antigen present (4×1 and 4×4) (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: The assay was able to reliably quantify cross-reactivity of monoclonal antibodies with up to four allelic variants of the same antigen.
source: On the above basis, we concluded that our assay was able to reliably quantify cross-reactivity of monoclonal antibodies with up to four allelic variants of the same antigen.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the validation experiments with multiple monoclonal antibodies.

claim: PBMC samples were from seven women with previous natural exposure to VAR2CSA-type PfEMP1 proteins during P. falciparum infection-exposed pregnancies.
source: In the final set of experiments, we applied the validated assay to the analysis of samples of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from seven women with previous natural exposure to VAR2CSA-type PfEMP1 proteins during P. falciparum infection-exposed pregnancies (mean parity: 4, range: 2–8).
evidence: This describes the sample characteristics used in the study.

claim: The mean parity of the women in the study was 4, with a range of 2–8.
source: In the final set of experiments, we applied the validated assay to the analysis of samples of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from seven women with previous natural exposure to VAR2CSA-type PfEMP1 proteins during P. falciparum infection-exposed pregnancies (mean parity: 4, range: 2–8).
evidence: This describes the sample characteristics used in the study.

claim: PBMCs from three sympatric men were included as negative controls.
source: PBMCs from three sympatric men were included as negative controls.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The frequencies of ASC secreting VAR2CSA-specific IgG tended to be higher among women than among the men.
source: The frequencies of ASC secreting VAR2CSA-specific IgG tended to be higher among women than among the men, where only low frequencies were detected (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The difference in VAR2CSA-specific IgG frequencies between women and men was statistically significant for the ID1-ID2 region only.
source: Although the difference was statistically significant for the ID1-ID2 region only (probably due to the low number of individuals tested), the pattern was the same for all the VAR2CSA regions tested and fully consistent with the well-established pregnancy-dependency of acquisition of substantial antibody reactivity to VAR2CSA.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Most of the spots detected in PBMC samples were single-colored.
source: Most of the spots detected were single-colored (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1), indicating that most corresponded to antibodies recognizing variant-specific epitopes not conserved among the tested allelic variants.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most antibodies in PBMC samples corresponded to antibodies recognizing variant-specific epitopes not conserved among the tested allelic variants.
source: Most of the spots detected were single-colored (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1), indicating that most corresponded to antibodies recognizing variant-specific epitopes not conserved among the tested allelic variants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing single-colored spots.

claim: No systematic differences in spot numbers or RSV values were detected between the 4×4 and 1×1 configurations for PBMC samples.
source: For five of the samples, sufficient cells were available to also test them in the 1×1 configuration. No systematic differences in spot numbers or RSV values were detected between the 4×4 and 1×1 configurations (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Clinical protection against malaria in areas with stable transmission of P. falciparum parasites is acquired in a piecemeal fashion over several years.
source: Clinical protection against malaria in areas with stable transmission of P. falciparum parasites is acquired in a piecemeal fashion over several years.
evidence: This is established knowledge about malaria immunity.

claim: Sterile protection following natural exposure to P. falciparum is very rarely achieved.
source: This slow rate of acquisition, and the fact that sterile protection following natural exposure is very rarely achieved, is often attributed to the very substantial polymorphic (allelic or inter-clonal) variation of the antigens that are important for protection (reviewed by Hviid, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to review by Hviid, 2005.

claim: Allelic variation represents an important immune-evasive strategy of the malaria parasites.
source: It is assumed that allelic variation represents an important immune-evasive strategy of the malaria parasites and that acquisition of broadly cross-reactive antibodies to key antigens following natural exposure is rare.
evidence: This is a commonly held assumption in the field.

claim: Acquisition of broadly cross-reactive antibodies to key antigens following natural exposure is rare.
source: It is assumed that allelic variation represents an important immune-evasive strategy of the malaria parasites and that acquisition of broadly cross-reactive antibodies to key antigens following natural exposure is rare.
evidence: This is a commonly held assumption in the field.

claim: Acquisition of protection to malaria is thought to rely on the accumulation of a broad repertoire of antibodies, which may each be variant-specific, but which together cover the repertoire of allelic antigen variants.
source: Instead, acquisition of protection is thought to rely on the accumulation of a broad repertoire of antibodies, which may each be variant-specific, but which together cover the repertoire of allelic antigen variants (Bull et al., 1998; Nielsen et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bull et al., 1998 and Nielsen et al., 2002.

claim: VAR2CSA-specific B cells that secrete broadly cross-reactive antibodies do exist.
source: This notwithstanding, it is evident that VAR2CSA-specific B cells that secrete broadly cross-reactive antibodies do exist.
evidence: This is supported by subsequent citations to studies showing cross-reactive antibodies.

claim: Memory B cells from women with natural exposure to placental malaria can be induced to secrete truly cross-reactive human monoclonal antibodies that are specific for VAR2CSA-type PfEMP1.
source: Thus, memory B cells from women with natural exposure to placental malaria can be induced to secrete truly cross-reactive human monoclonal antibodies that are specific for VAR2CSA-type PfEMP1—in fact, all of the monoclonal antibodies described showed substantial allelic variant cross-reactivity (Barfod et al., 2007; Barfod et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barfod et al., 2007 and Barfod et al., 2010.

claim: All of the monoclonal antibodies described by Barfod et al. showed substantial allelic variant cross-reactivity.
source: Thus, memory B cells from women with natural exposure to placental malaria can be induced to secrete truly cross-reactive human monoclonal antibodies that are specific for VAR2CSA-type PfEMP1—in fact, all of the monoclonal antibodies described showed substantial allelic variant cross-reactivity (Barfod et al., 2007; Barfod et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barfod et al., 2007 and Barfod et al., 2010.

claim: VAR2CSA contains conserved epitopes.
source: VAR2CSA thus contains conserved epitopes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the existence of cross-reactive antibodies.

claim: The IT4, NF54, M920, and Malayan Camp strains were chosen because they are geographically and temporally distant.
source: These strains were chosen because they are geographically and temporally distant, and because their amino acid sequences belong to distinct phylogenetic clusters (Renn et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the rationale for strain selection, supported by citation.

claim: The amino acid sequences of IT4, NF54, M920, and Malayan Camp belong to distinct phylogenetic clusters.
source: These strains were chosen because they are geographically and temporally distant, and because their amino acid sequences belong to distinct phylogenetic clusters (Renn et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Renn et al., 2021.

claim: DBL3X and DBL5ε appear to be dominant targets of naturally acquired and truly cross-reactive VAR2CSA-specific IgG.
source: DBL3X and DBL5ε were chosen as they appear to be dominant targets of naturally acquired and truly cross-reactive VAR2CSA-specific IgG (Barfod et al., 2010), while the ID1-ID2 region was selected because it includes the above-mentioned minimal binding region used as antigen in the recent vaccine trials (Mordmüller et al., 2019; Sirima et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barfod et al., 2010.

claim: The ID1-ID2 region includes the minimal binding region used as antigen in recent vaccine trials.
source: DBL3X and DBL5ε were chosen as they appear to be dominant targets of naturally acquired and truly cross-reactive VAR2CSA-specific IgG (Barfod et al., 2010), while the ID1-ID2 region was selected because it includes the above-mentioned minimal binding region used as antigen in the recent vaccine trials (Mordmüller et al., 2019; Sirima et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mordmüller et al., 2019 and Sirima et al., 2020.

claim: The minimal binding domain is defined as the shortest contiguous part of VAR2CSA that retains the affinity of the full-length molecule for oncofetal CSA.
source: It is defined as the shortest contiguous part of VAR2CSA that retains the affinity of the full-length molecule for the VAR2CSA cognate receptor, oncofetal CSA (Clausen et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Clausen et al., 2012.

claim: The multiplexed reverse FluoroSpot assay has previously been applied to studying the reactivity of monoclonal antibodies against four serotypes of dengue virus (DENV-1 to DENV-4).
source: The multiplexed reverse FluoroSpot assay has previously been applied to studying the reactivity of monoclonal antibodies against four serotypes of dengue virus (DENV-1 to DENV-4) (Adam et al., 2018; Hadjilaou et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Adam et al., 2018 and Hadjilaou et al., 2015.

claim: The assay described by Jahnmatz et al. has been successfully applied to simultaneous detection of B cells secreting antibodies specific for differently tagged antigens from three different pathogens.
source: That version of the assay has been successfully applied to simultaneous detection of B cells secreting antibodies specific for differently tagged antigens from three different pathogens (Jahnmatz et al., 2020a) and for four distinct P. falciparum antigens (Jahnmatz et al., 2020b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jahnmatz et al., 2020a.

claim: The assay described by Jahnmatz et al. has been successfully applied to simultaneous detection of B cells secreting antibodies specific for four distinct P. falciparum antigens.
source: That version of the assay has been successfully applied to simultaneous detection of B cells secreting antibodies specific for differently tagged antigens from three different pathogens (Jahnmatz et al., 2020a) and for four distinct P. falciparum antigens (Jahnmatz et al., 2020b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jahnmatz et al., 2020b.

claim: The assay has not previously been used for the analysis of antibody cross-reactivity to allelic variants of a single antigen.
source: The assay has not previously been used for the analysis of antibody cross-reactivity to allelic variants of a single antigen, which is more demanding in terms of specificity (ability to distinguish between allelic variants rather than different antigens altogether).
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current application.

claim: Most of the B cells that secreted antibodies recognizing the test antigens only recognized a single allelic variant.
source: Most of the B cells that secreted antibodies recognizing our test antigens only recognized a single allelic variant.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PBMC experiments.

claim: The finding that most B cells only recognized a single allelic variant is in agreement with a previous study by Doritchamou et al., 2016.
source: This finding is in agreement with a previous study (Doritchamou et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Doritchamou et al., 2016.

claim: Doritchamou et al. sequentially depleted immune sera of reactivity with allelic variants of ID1-ID2 and DBL5ε.
source: The authors of the earlier study sequentially depleted immune sera of reactivity with allelic variants of ID1-ID2 and DBL5ε (and of DBL4ε, not included in our study).
evidence: This describes the methods used in the cited study.

claim: Doritchamou et al. concluded that allelic cross-reactivity of VAR2CSA-specific IgG appears to be very limited.
source: They concluded, like we do here, using a fundamentally different approach, that allelic cross-reactivity of VAR2CSA-specific IgG appears to be very limited.
evidence: This is a comparison with conclusions from a cited study.

claim: Limited allelic cross-reactivity would explain the very limited cross-reactivity observed in the recent VAR2CSA vaccine trials.
source: This would explain the very limited cross-reactivity observed in the recent VAR2CSA vaccine trials (Mordmüller et al., 2019; Sirima et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the study findings to vaccine trial results, supported by citations.

claim: Doritchamou et al., 2022 reported a new study employing allelic variants of the full ectodomain of VAR2CSA.
source: While the current study was in progress, Doritchamou et al., 2022 reported a new study, using the same approach as in their earlier study (Doritchamou et al., 2016), but now employing allelic variants of the full ectodomain of VAR2CSA (Renn et al., 2021) rather than the single- and oligo-domain antigens used previously (and here).
evidence: Supported by citation to Doritchamou et al., 2022.

claim: The new study by Doritchamou et al., 2022 indicated a very marked cross-reactivity of VAR2CSA-specific antibodies.
source: The new study indicated a very marked cross-reactivity of VAR2CSA-specific antibodies, as depletion on a single allelic variant resulted in almost complete loss of reactivity with the other variants.
evidence: This describes findings from the cited study.

claim: The finding of marked cross-reactivity by Doritchamou et al., 2022 is in stark contrast to the findings reported in the current study.
source: This finding is in stark contrast to those reported here as well as in the authors' own earlier study.
evidence: This is a comparison of findings between studies.

claim: The finding of marked cross-reactivity by Doritchamou et al., 2022 agrees with earlier reports that VAR2CSA-specific memory B cells tend to secrete broadly cross-reactive antibodies.
source: However, it agrees very well with our earlier reports (Barfod et al., 2007; Barfod et al., 2010) that VAR2CSA-specific memory B cells generated in response to natural parasite exposure tend to secrete antibodies that are broadly cross-reactive.
evidence: Supported by citations to Barfod et al., 2007 and Barfod et al., 2010.

claim: Broadly cross-reactive antibodies to VAR2CSA target conformational epitopes that are not properly reproduced by smaller antigens consisting of domains or regions of the larger, full-length protein.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that broadly cross-reactive antibodies to VAR2CSA and probably to other PfEMP1 antigens—indeed, possibly to many complex, high-molecular weight proteins—target conformational epitopes that are not properly reproduced by smaller antigens consisting of domains or regions of the larger, full-length protein.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing results across multiple studies.

claim: Some cross-reactive epitopes are likely to be composed of amino acids that are far apart in the primary sequence of the protein.
source: Some of these—such as the epitope of the monoclonal antibody PAM1.4, which recognizes the full ectodomain of most VAR2CSA variants but not any of its constituent domains individually (Barfod et al., 2007)—are likely to be composed of amino acids that are far apart in the primary sequence of the protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of PAM1.4, supported by citation.

claim: What determines the fine specificity of antibodies elicited after exposure to native complex antigens may not be the same as that determining fine specificity after subunit vaccination.
source: It also suggests that what determines the fine specificity of antibodies elicited after exposure to native complex antigens may not be the same as that determining fine specificity after subunit vaccination, even when those antibodies all recognize epitopes within the construct used for vaccination.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the contrasting results with different antigen formats.

claim: The developed assay is suitable for the interrogation of the degree of allelic cross-reactivity of monoclonal antibodies.
source: In conclusion, we have developed an assay that is suitable for the interrogation of the degree of allelic cross-reactivity of monoclonal antibodies.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the validation and application of the assay.

claim: The assay may be applied to deeper investigations of how antibody fine specificity is determined.
source: However, our results indicate that it may also be applied to deeper investigations of how antibody fine specificity (including variant specificity versus cross-reactivity) is determined.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential future applications of the assay.

claim: The main caveat of the study is that it involved only a relatively small number of individuals.
source: The main caveat with respect to the conclusions drawn here is that our work was mainly a methods development study and therefore involved only a relatively small number of individuals.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a study limitation.

claim: Larger studies should be undertaken to assess the robustness of the preliminary conclusions regarding the frequency of allelic cross-reactivity in pregnant women naturally exposed to P. falciparum infection.
source: Larger studies should be undertaken to assess the robustness of our preliminary conclusions regarding the frequency of allelic cross-reactivity in pregnant women naturally exposed to P. falciparum infection.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.
